kp.k: Field study tested tools and additional adoption support
kp.d: Chien and Kim report a fall 2023 baseline survey of 202 legal aid professionals and a pilot beginning with 91 participants, offered access to ChatGPT-4, Gavel, and, for eligible California organizations, CoCounsel. Access durations varied, extending up to two months. Ten participants dropped out; 81 finished, and 66 completed the exit survey. The randomized comparison concerned concierge support, not AI access versus no AI access: 54 initially entered the standard group and 37 the concierge group, with participants from the same organization assigned together to limit spillovers. Gavel included traditional automation rather than solely generative AI.
qs: Two hundred and two people completed the initial survey, and 91 people began the pilot.
Our pilot included three AI tools that include automation, “traditional AI,” and generative AI capabilities and that could, in principle, be used by lawyers or consumers.

kp.k: Most respondents reported productivity gains and continued-use intentions
kp.d: Among post-pilot respondents, approximately 90% reported some productivity increase, 86% increased AI use, and 63% greater satisfaction. Seventy-five percent intended continued use, and 62.5% intended paid use. Comparable pre/post responses showed reported uses increasing from 1.2 to 4.2 (p < .001). These are participant self-assessments and intentions, not independently measured increases in completed cases or subsequent purchases. The text reports 25% experiencing medium or significant productivity gains, but its footnote separately lists 21% medium and 14% significant, an unresolved internal discrepancy.
qs: 86% reported more AI use during the pilot, and 63% reported greater satisfaction with AI after the pilot (Table 1).
Among the tested tools, legal aid professionals favored ChatGPT, even over higher priced and specialized products (Figure 3).
Breakdown: 9% no increase, 50% a little bit of an increase, 21% a medium increase, 14% a significant increase.

kp.k: Study design limits causal and generalizable productivity conclusions
kp.d: The authors acknowledge self-reporting bias, the absence of standardized performance tasks, a short pre/post observation window, and rapidly evolving tools. Pilot participation was self-selected and skewed younger and less experienced than the baseline sample; 47.6% held leadership roles. About 41 participants supplied use cases, requested specifically as helpful examples. Some missing demographics were inferred using LinkedIn, visual inspection, and probabilistic classifiers. The appendix lists 204 baseline respondents whereas the main study reports 202. Recommendations are explicitly preliminary.
qs: While this made it impossible for us to assess performance gains or losses with reference to a standardized task, we were still able to assess participant experiences with the tools in a few ways.
This self-selecting group had demographic traits that differed from the complete survey group, skewing younger and less experienced.
viewed as preliminary, due to the limited scope of our survey and pilot study, warranting further research, inquiry, and refinement.

kp.k: Initial gender adoption differences disappeared in post-pilot comparisons
kp.d: In the baseline survey, men reported current AI use more frequently than women, 47% versus 17% (p = .001); 50% of women versus 28% of men were uncertain about or did not plan future use. Within the pilot subgroup, initial use was 65% among men and 22% among women. Post-pilot outcomes showed no statistically significant gender differences across reported use, productivity, satisfaction, concerns, output quality, and future-use intentions. The authors interpret this as supporting equitable exposure and outreach, particularly because women constitute most legal aid workers; the result is absence of statistically significant differences, not proof of universal equivalence.
qs: Women’s outlook regarding the future use of tools was also less optimistic—50% of women were unsure of or not planning to use AI tools in their work in the future as compared to 28% of men.
This suggests that once men and women were equally exposed to and provided with the tools, there was no statistically significant difference in their reported experiences.

kp.k: Concierge support improved selected reported outcomes
kp.d: Support comprised weekly use-case emails, office hours, tailored vendor training, and curated materials. Exit-survey comparisons involved 41 standard-group and 25 concierge-group respondents. Table A2 reports any productivity improvement for 84% versus 100%, output-quality ratings of 1.6 versus 1.9, and positive job-impact expectations of 62% versus 88%. After adjustment for previous AI use, output quality, productivity intensity, and positive job outlook remained significant at p < .05 or better. Satisfaction and paid-use intentions had only marginal unadjusted significance, while frequency and future use were not statistically significant; the broad introductory claims should therefore be read alongside the detailed table.
qs: But on every other met- ric, pilot participants who received concierge services reported better outcomes than those that did not.
For five out of the nine outcomes, the differences were statistically significant.
The differences were not large, but they were significant on a number of metrics.

kp.k: Useful applications concentrated on lower-risk, supervised tasks
kp.d: The companion database contains approximately 100 helpful use cases with prompts and outputs. Participants reported average efficiency gains of 50% across submitted tasks, with some examples reaching 80%; these are selected, self-reported task estimates rather than profession-wide productivity measurements. Promising applications included summarizing supplied documents, brainstorming discovery, drafting correspondence and agreements, adjusting tone, and administrative writing. Grounding outputs in user-provided material reduced but did not eliminate error risks. No submitted use cases involved brief writing or other complex legal writing.
qs: There were no use cases submitted for brief writing or other complex legal writing.
This includes document summaries and brainstorming and ideation.
Some of the “Other” use cases that did not clearly fall within an- other category included coding, database administration, and HR.

kp.k: Research and translation benefits remained conditional on checking
kp.d: Legal research usefulness varied substantially. Participants reported benefits from preliminary overviews and checking research already conducted conventionally: an asylum-related CoCounsel example reportedly saved 20%, while quick clinic research reportedly improved efficiency by 40%. More complex questions about legal hierarchy sometimes saved no time and were rated unlikely to be reused. Translation also required revision: one Spanish client-communication example reportedly improved efficiency by 20% despite an unsatisfactory initial translation. Plain-language explanations were another useful means of improving accessibility.
qs: CoCounsel provided a short memo, which correctly con- cluded there was no clear case law.
“always double check the translation,”
ChatGPT-4’s simplification of legalese was also rated as extremely useful (e.g., ex- plaining a trust).

kp.k: Persistent risks require confidentiality safeguards and human verification
kp.d: More than 70% remained equally or more concerned after the pilot, despite reported benefits. Principal concerns included confidentiality, data privacy, inaccurate results, and hallucinations. The authors report California State Bar guidance requiring appropriate security, protection or anonymization of client information, and verification and correction of generated analysis and citations. Participants often omitted identifying client information. Court sanctions incidents, including Mata v. Avianca, illustrate failures to verify fabricated authorities; they are not measurements of model error rates.
qs: Even if the product does not utilize or share inputted in- formation, it may lack reasonable or adequate security.
A lawyer must not input any confidential information of the client into any generative AI solution that lacks adequate confidentiality and security protections.
While pilot participants reported time savings of up to 80% on certain tasks, they also emphasized the need to verify, correct, and/or supplement AI-generated outputs.

kp.k: Authors favor lawyer augmentation rather than professional replacement
kp.d: The authors recommend AI as an assistant that accelerates drafting and nonlegal work while lawyers retain judgment, empathy, supervision, and approval. A clinic anecdote describes generating customized letters within a 60-minute appointment after client and attorney consent, with supervising counsel reviewing the result. Approximately 71% expected positive substitution of job elements. The source inconsistently allocates the remaining responses: its main discussion gives 26% no replacement and 3% negative impact, while footnote 161 reverses these categories. These outlook responses are not observed employment outcomes.
qs: We recommend that legal aid see generative AI as a powerful assistant to lawyers, not as a replacement, ensuring that legal services become more accessible while retaining the essential human expertise and empathy that is central to legal aid.
This enabled the LCCR attorney to provide the client with a customized letter by the end of the appointment, resulting in faster and better work product for clinic clients.

kp.k: Access-to-justice gains require more than individual lawyer efficiency
kp.d: Drawing on Legal Services Corporation evidence, the article describes 92% of substantial civil legal needs among low-income Americans as unmet and distinguishes a knowledge gap from insufficient service capacity. It cites only 2.8 paid legal aid lawyers per 10,000 residents in poverty. Housing, expungement, and immigration examples establish the stakes of inadequate help, while acknowledging that associations between representation and outcomes are not necessarily causal. The pilot investigates workforce augmentation, not a measured reduction in the overall justice gap.
qs: Paid legal assistance is often out of reach and legal aid organizations can only serve about 30% of the clients that come through their doors.
While correlation is not causation, and even the best lawyer cannot guarantee victory, in adversarial contexts, the absence of counsel is generally associated with worse outcomes.

kp.k: Affordability and implementation support shape equitable adoption
kp.d: The authors recommend nonprofit discounts or free access, procurement and implementation funding, and targeted outreach, especially to women. Numerous respondents conditioned continued use on organizational affordability. At the trial, listed monthly seat prices were approximately $20 for ChatGPT-4, $165 for Gavel's standard package, and $400 for CoCounsel. Proposed shared support includes a national legal aid technology help desk, communities of practice, and 'Tech Bono' collaboration among technical professionals, lawyers, and students. These are recommendations informed by reported adoption barriers, not evaluated nationwide interventions.
qs: Our findings indicate that simply making generative AI tools “available” does not guarantee equitable or optimal outcomes.

62.5% of pilot participants reported that they would continue to use paid AI tools for work (Table 2), but numerous respondents said they would only continue using the tools if their organizations could afford them.

An exten- sion of the pro bono model would be for engineers and law students to work together with organizations to serve not only individual clients, but clients at scale through automation and AI tools.

kp.k: Lawyer-directed consumer tools offer prospective scaling beyond clinics
kp.d: The authors argue that consumer-facing systems combining generative AI, automation, and human oversight may expand coverage more dramatically than equipping individual lawyers alone. Illustrations include Rentervention's tenant guidance and document workflows, Rasa's technology-assisted expungement services, and AILA/Visalaw.Ai's GEN 1.0 lawyer-facing immigration research product, launched January 2024. Rentervention's reported 50,000 renters helped since 2019 and Rasa founder Noella Sudbury's reported nearly 10,000 first-year users are externally reported service counts, not controlled evidence isolating generative AI's contribution; GEN is not presented as direct consumer representation.
qs: “Rentervention has helped more than 50,000 renters since 2019,”
“close to 10,000 people used [their] services (in comparison to 400 people per year served by legal aid).”
These solutions can serve as inspiration for further discussion, research, and development of le- gal aid-directed technologies.

kp.k: Regulatory experimentation could support certified legal aid bots
kp.d: The article frames unauthorized-practice restrictions as consumer protection that may also obstruct innovation and technology investment. It distinguishes Utah's supervised regulatory sandbox from Arizona's alternative-business-structure reforms and describes limited-scope community justice worker programs. The authors recommend exploring these models for legal aid technology and voluntary state-bar certification of bots, covering accuracy, currency, ethical issues, transparency, privacy, and confidentiality. These are proposed safeguards, not existing general authorization or demonstrated certification effectiveness.
qs: Arizona’s regulatory reform efforts, without a sandbox per se, consist of the state adopting a framework that allows alternative busi- ness structures for law firms.
Lawyers and tech- nologists could collaborate on appropriate certification standards and procedures tailored for verifying legal bots across domains and dimen- sions.

kp.k: Unequal access and biased outputs could worsen disparities
kp.d: The authors caution that specialized legal tools may preferentially serve well-resourced users and that poorer consumers could receive inferior AI assistance. They report Drew Simshaw's warning about a two-tier system and cite limited digital access, algorithmic literacy, and discriminatory outputs as additional risks. A cited Noam Kolt study found GPT-3 correctly answered 77% of 200 consumer-contract questions, but performance varied with wording and was poorer on pro-consumer questions. These are contextual findings and warnings, not harms measured in this legal aid pilot.
qs: technology often fails to be a leveler
Performance was also highly sensitive to the wording of questions.
“while language models have the potential to empower consumers, they also have the potential to provide mis- leading advice and entrench harmful biases.”

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Chien and Kim claim that supervised AI use can improve legal aid professionals’ productivity, that assistance improves adoption outcomes, and that lawyer-directed technological services may expand coverage beyond individual lawyer augmentation.
pts.d: The authors report that approximately 90% of exit-survey respondents experienced some productivity increase and 75% intended to continue using AI. Across submitted beneficial use cases, participants estimated an average efficiency increase of 50%, with savings up to 80% on particular tasks. These are participant estimates, not measured increases in overall organizational capacity. Beneficial applications included summarization, brainstorming, preliminary or confirmatory research, first drafts, accessible communications, document automation, fundraising, and administrative work. The authors favor augmentation rather than replacement of lawyers. They report that baseline gender differences in uptake were not statistically significant in post-pilot outcomes and that concierge support improved several outcomes. They also argue that making tools available alone does not ensure equitable adoption. Beyond individual assistance, they predict that lawyer-directed consumer-facing solutions combining generative AI, automation, and human oversight may dramatically increase service coverage. They propose support infrastructure, funding, outreach, and voluntary bot certification as ways to enable these benefits.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The principal evidence consists of a baseline survey, a short field pilot with randomized support, participant-submitted use cases, and illustrative service-provider examples.
pts.d: The main text reports 202 baseline respondents, 91 pilot entrants, 81 finishers, and 66 exit-survey respondents; the appendix instead refers to 204 baseline respondents. Approximately 41 participants supplied use cases. Participants received access to ChatGPT-4 and Gavel, with CoCounsel available to an eligible subset. The study randomized concierge support rather than access to AI versus no AI; it describes individual enrollee randomization while keeping participants from the same organization in the same group. Exit responses came from 41 standard-support and 25 concierge participants. Table A2 reports adjusted differences favoring concierge support in perceived output quality, degree of productivity increase, and positive job outlook at conventional significance thresholds. Satisfaction and future paid-use differences were marginally significant only in the unadjusted table; frequency of use was not statistically significant. Productivity, output quality, and future use were self-reported, and the authors explicitly acknowledge reporting bias and the absence of standardized performance measurement. The 100-use-case collection illustrates selected helpful applications rather than a representative task benchmark. Examples include an attorney reporting that an eviction notice was rescinded after an AI-assisted accommodation letter and an author's clinic experience producing customized letters for supervising-lawyer approval. For larger-scale delivery, the authors cite Rentervention's reported assistance to more than 50,000 renters since 2019 and Rasa founder Noella Sudbury's account of nearly 10,000 first-year users versus 400 annually served by legal aid. These service totals are illustrative rather than estimates isolating generative AI's contribution. The paper also draws on earlier legal-task experiments and regulatory literature. Some headline figures are internally inconsistent: the prose reports 25% with medium or significant productivity gains while a footnote lists 21% medium and 14% significant; the job-outlook prose and footnote reverse the 26% and 3% categories for neutral versus negative expectations.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The findings concern a late-2023 pilot with short follow-up; broader access-to-justice effects are conditional projections without a quantified deadline.
pts.d: Baseline recruitment occurred in fall 2023, pilot enrollment ran from November 3 to November 29, 2023, and exit submissions were requested by January 12, 2024. Access lasted approximately one to two months, varying by participant and tool, with two to three months between surveys. Intentions to continue use do not establish sustained adoption or subsequent client-service expansion. The authors condition useful deployment on task selection, supervision, verification, confidentiality protections, affordability, and assistance in overcoming learning costs. Participants favored first drafts, grounded summaries, lower-stakes administrative tasks, and preliminary or confirmatory research rather than autonomous complex legal analysis. Research quality varied with complexity, and translations required checking and revision. Over 70% remained equally or more concerned about AI after the pilot. The authors describe recommendations as preliminary given the study's limited scope. Their near-term expectation is continued professional intermediation because of regulatory constraints. Scalable consumer-facing services and certification are proposed future directions requiring quality controls and, where appropriate, regulatory reform, not demonstrated consequences of the pilot.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claims primarily concern nonprofit legal aid workers and underserved clients, with distinct implications for women, resource-constrained organizations, volunteers, and consumer-facing service developers.
pts.d: The target population is legal aid professionals, predominantly lawyers, rather than commercial law firms generally. Leadership roles accounted for 47.6% of pilot participants, helping explain the prominence of fundraising, communications, HR, and administrative applications. Supervisors reported greater productivity improvements than nonsupervisory respondents; the study did not find significant productivity differences by gender, race, age, or legal experience. Women were less likely than men to report baseline AI use—17% versus 47% in the overall survey—but post-pilot reported outcomes were not statistically distinguishable. The authors treat this as especially important in a female-majority legal aid workforce, without establishing that all gender disparities have been eliminated. Resource-constrained organizations may need discounted access, funding, and shared technical support; continued paid use was conditional on affordability for numerous respondents. Volunteers may benefit from guided document workflows and support. Intended ultimate beneficiaries include low-income tenants, people seeking expungement, immigrants, and clients facing language or literacy barriers. The authors link greater lawyer capacity and accessible information to potentially narrower unmet legal need, but do not measure an aggregate reduction in that need. Vendors, funders, bar authorities, technologists, and law students are assigned enabling roles in access programs, assistance, development, and quality assurance. The authors also warn that unequal resources and digital literacy could produce inferior AI assistance for poorer users rather than equitable improvement.
